title: Restaurant
description: A small restaurant: menu sections with prices, kitchen notes, opening hours and contact.

restaurant.title: A short menu, rewritten on the mornings it needs to be
restaurant.tagline: Fourteen covers off Picton Street, Bristol. Most of the list holds all year; the rest depends on what the market had at six.
restaurant.intro:
Marrow & Salt is one room, an open pass and a wood oven that was here when we took the lease.

We cook what keeps: braises, whole vegetables, bread, one fish. The kitchen is three people, so the menu is deliberately shorter than the room could carry.

## How dinner runs

Small plates arrive as they are ready rather than in courses. Two or three each, then something from the grill to share, is how most tables eat and how the portions are built.

We hold four seats at the counter for walk-ins every night, including Saturday.

menu.name: Breakfast
menu.summary: Weekends until noon. Bread, eggs, one thing from the oven, and coffee that is not an afterthought.
menu.body:
Breakfast exists because the oven is already hot on a Saturday and it seemed wasteful not to use it.

Eggs come from a farm outside Chew Magna, delivered twice a week. The bread is the same dough we bake for dinner, shaped smaller.

We do not take breakfast bookings. The room turns quickly and the wait is rarely more than fifteen minutes.

Toasted, with whatever fruit is in

menu.name: Small plates
menu.summary: The part of the menu that changes most. Three each is a sensible start for two people.
menu.body:
These are written on the board most weeks and printed only when they settle.

Vegetables lead here, not because of a position on eating but because the market two streets away is better at vegetables than it is at anything else.

## Allergens

Ask and we will tell you exactly what is in a dish. We do not print symbols; the recipes move too often for the print to stay honest.

menu.name: Sandwiches
menu.summary: Friday lunch only, twelve to three. One meat, one vegetable, both in our own bread.
menu.body:
Friday lunch started as staff food and stayed on because people kept knocking on the window.

It is a short list and it sells out. When the bread is gone, lunch is over — usually around half past two.

Everything is available to take away, wrapped, at the same price.

menu.name: From the grill
menu.summary: Cooked over wood, meant for the middle of the table. One order feeds two comfortably.
menu.body:
The grill runs on beech and a little oak. It takes forty minutes to be usable and about four hours to be at its best, which is why we open at six and not at five.

Meat comes whole from a farm near Chepstow and is butchered here. That is the reason the list is short: we use the animal we have, in the order the cuts are ready.

Everything from this section rests for at least ten minutes, so it will not be the first thing to reach your table.

items.detail: In the fat from the grill

menu.name: Puddings
menu.summary: Three, made in the afternoon. When they are gone they are gone.
menu.body:
We are not a pastry kitchen and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Three puddings is what one person can make well between lunch and service.

The custard is the same recipe for all of them, which is either laziness or focus depending on the evening.

menu.name: Wine & cider
menu.summary: Thirty bottles, half of them from the west of England. Six open by the glass each week.
menu.body:
The list is short because the cellar is a cupboard. The upside is that we have drunk everything on it.

Cider is treated like wine here — served in a glass, at cellar temperature, from producers within an hour's drive.

Corkage is £15 and we will happily open something you brought.

notes.title: Why the coffee stayed the same
notes.standfirst: Eight years, one roaster. We tried to change it three times and the room noticed every time.
notes.body:
Coffee was meant to be the thing that came after dinner, not a second business.

Our roaster is twenty minutes away and delivers weekly. Two cheaper offers arrived last year and we ran both for a fortnight. Both times the same question came back across the counter: has the coffee changed?

Being noticed is information. We went back.

notes.title: Fourteen covers, and why not more
notes.standfirst: The room fits twenty-two. We took six tables out and kept the counter.
notes.body:
Three of us cook. The number of plates three people can send out properly in one service is a fixed number and we found it by counting, not guessing.

At twenty-two covers the wait between small plates and the grill stretched past twenty minutes. At fourteen it sits under eight.

## Bookings

Half the room is bookable and half is held for walk-ins. The counter is never bookable, which is the only rule we have never bent.

notes.title: Where the bread flour comes from
notes.standfirst: One mill in Wiltshire, one variety, bought a season at a time.
notes.body:
Buying a season of flour at once carries an obvious risk: a poor harvest means twelve months of living with it.

We do it anyway. A bakery that switches flour drifts week to week, and finding out why takes days you do not have during service.

We visit the mill each autumn. Not as a trip — to see the crop and agree the grind.

notes.title: We took the pasta off
notes.standfirst: Two seasons on the menu. It sold well, which is exactly why it went.
notes.body:
Pasta leaves the pass fast, carries a good margin and nobody complains about it. That is the problem: once a third of the room ordered it, the grill sat half-used at nine o'clock.

A kitchen is defined by the easiest dish on its menu. Take that away and what is left is what you actually do.

It may come back one winter, as a single dish.

notes.title: No service charge
notes.standfirst: It is in the prices. The bill has no line you did not choose.
notes.body:
The number on the menu is the number you pay. No cover, no bread charge, no discretionary percentage.

There is one reason for this: the arithmetic that happens when the bill lands undoes most of what the meal built.

Tips go to the room and are shared weekly. The kitchen is in that share.

notes.title: Saturday night is walk-in only
notes.standfirst: Six nights take bookings. Saturday belongs to whoever is on the street.
notes.body:
Saturday is the night people walk up Picton Street and look in. For the two seasons we took bookings, the room filled three days ahead and we turned away everyone who did that.

Now the door is open. After eight there may be a wait; you can sit at the counter and order small plates while you do.

In summer the front tables go early — arriving at half past six works.
